Beginners are welcome—enthusiasm, reliability, and good communication matter more than having every skill already.
summary:
PosturePilot is an offline-first, gravity-aware health-monitoring system that helps astronauts understand and act on their health during long missions—no cloud, cameras, or Earth contact needed.

Crew-entered indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood) combine with optional ESP32 smart-seat data (pressure array + IMU). The dashboard shows trends, color-coded status, plain-language guidance, an interactive body map, and adaptive reminders for measurements, breaks, and exercise.

Its core is the Movement-Debt Index (MDI)—a transparent, personalized score that rises with prolonged stillness and pressure concentration, and falls after verified breaks or logged exercise. Breaks are verified by app confirmation or detected chair movement. MDI adjusts for microgravity, lunar, Martian, or Earth gravity. PosturePilot supports self-assessment; it does not diagnose or prescribe.

An untrusted-edge, trusted-core design lets the habitat dashboard validate every data frame via CRC checks, sequence numbers, timestamps, and plausibility rules. A watchdog, current monitoring, load switch, and fail-off haptics provide fault tolerance; if electronics fail, the seat remains an ordinary ergonomic chair.

A gravity-mode simulator with fault injection enables demonstration without flight hardware. Validation will measure posture-classification accuracy, static-posture detection, break compliance, discomfort, engagement, and crew-time burden
details:
PosturePilot: Smart Seat Health Monitoring System is an offline-first, gravity-aware health-monitoring platform that helps astronauts understand their own health indicators, maintain movement and recovery routines, and respond early to personal changes during long-duration missions. It is designed for the isolation, confinement, communication delays, and altered gravity of deep-space travel, where crew members may have limited support from Earth and must take greater responsibility for monitoring their own well-being.

What it does

PosturePilot combines crew-entered health indicators with optional passive data from a smart seat. Crew members can log heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep duration, and mood. The dashboard compares these values with each person’s own baseline and displays trends, color-coded status, plain-language explanations, and an interactive body map that links indicators to relevant body regions.

An optional ESP32-based smart seat uses a pressure-sensor array and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to detect seated posture, pressure distribution, prolonged stillness, chair movement, and sitting duration. The system identifies patterns such as slouching, forward lean, lateral lean, asymmetric loading, and extended periods without meaningful movement.

The central feature is the Movement-Debt Index (MDI): a transparent, personalized score that increases with prolonged uninterrupted static time and unfavorable pressure concentration, then decreases after verified movement breaks or logged exercise-countermeasure sessions. Breaks can be verified through app confirmation or detected chair movement. The MDI is adjusted for the selected gravity environment—microgravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, or Earth gravity—to provide context-aware movement and recovery recommendations.

PosturePilot provides adaptive reminders for routine measurements, posture changes, stand-up breaks, stretching, and exercise sessions. It supports self-assessment and healthy routine adherence, but it does not diagnose medical conditions, prescribe treatment, or replace professional medical care.

How it works

The system follows an untrusted-edge, trusted-core architecture. The ESP32 seat node collects sensor data, performs basic filtering and signal-quality checks, classifies simple posture states, calculates local movement indicators, and temporarily stores data when the habitat network is unavailable. The crew tablet or habitat computer acts as the trusted core: it validates every incoming data frame using cyclic redundancy checks (CRC), sequence numbers, timestamps, and plausibility rules before using the data in the dashboard.

The ESP32 also hosts a lightweight local web server, allowing crew members to access the dashboard through a habitat-local network without relying on cloud services or Earth communication. The dashboard can run in an offline mode, while optional synchronization can occur only when a crew member explicitly enables it.

Radiation protection is built into the system design. The ESP32 and associated electronics are treated as commercial off-the-shelf components rather than radiation-hardened parts. The seat node includes an external watchdog, independent current monitoring, current limiting, a load switch, and thermal monitoring to reduce risks associated with hardware faults and radiation-induced single-event latch-up. Data integrity is protected through CRC checks, sequence numbers, timestamps, retransmission, and encrypted local buffering. Haptic outputs are designed to fail safely, and if the electronics fail, the seat continues to function as a conventional ergonomic chair.

A gravity-mode simulator and fault-injection mode allow the complete system to be demonstrated and tested without flight hardware. The simulator can model different gravity environments and simulate sensor-node faults, communication interruptions, corrupted data frames, and loss of power.

Benefits

PosturePilot helps crew members:

  • Understand personal health trends through clear visual dashboards.
  • Maintain healthier sitting, movement, and recovery habits.
  • Detect prolonged static posture and increasing movement debt.
  • Complete routine health measurements and exercise sessions.
  • Receive private, non-intrusive reminders through haptic feedback and visual cues.
  • Protect privacy through local processing and no camera or microphone.
  • Operate without cloud connectivity or continuous communication with Earth.
  • Continue using the chair safely if the smart electronics fail.

The system is designed to reduce the burden of health self-monitoring. Instead of requiring astronauts to remember every measurement or interpret isolated numbers, PosturePilot brings indicators together in one dashboard and provides simple, actionable prompts.

Intended impact

PosturePilot is intended to support astronaut health, comfort, and performance during long-duration missions by helping crews maintain movement, recovery routines, and awareness of personal health trends. It addresses NASA’s human-spaceflight hazards of isolation and confinement, hostile or closed environments, and gravity-related reductions in cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness.

The project can initially support analog astronauts, isolation-study facilities, polar and high-altitude research teams, remote workers, and people who spend long periods seated. Its longer-term pathway is a privacy-preserving crew-health and movement-support dashboard for lunar surface habitats and Mars missions.

By making health data visible, understandable, and actionable, PosturePilot aims to help crew members make timely, informed decisions about their own well-being while preserving privacy and operational autonomy.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

Hardware

  • ESP32 development module for local sensing, control, and web-server hosting
  • Pressure-sensor array for seat and backrest posture detection
  • IMU for chair movement, recline angle, and stillness detection
  • Optional load cells for left-right weight balance
  • Vibration motors for private haptic feedback
  • RGB LED for visual status feedback
  • External watchdog, current monitor, current-limiting circuit, load switch, and thermal sensor for fault protection
  • Optional tablet or habitat computer for the main dashboard

Software and coding languages

  • MicroPython or Arduino C/C++ for ESP32 firmware
  • Python for data processing, baseline modeling, and prototype analysis
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the local web dashboard
  • Flutter or React Native for a mobile or tablet companion application
  • SQLite or local encrypted storage for offline data storage
  • TensorFlow Lite Micro for optional lightweight on-device posture classification
  • Figma for user-interface design
  • Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration

Data and validation tools

  • NASA Human Research Program resources for mission hazards and health-risk context
  • Open human-activity and posture datasets for initial model development
  • Custom data collected from the PosturePilot prototype for calibration and validation
  • A gravity-mode simulator for testing recommendations across gravity environments
  • Fault-injection testing to evaluate system recovery, data integrity, and fail-safe behavior

Creativity and innovation

PosturePilot is creative because it does not treat health monitoring as a collection of isolated numbers. Instead, it connects crew-entered health indicators with passive movement and loading data to create a more complete picture of daily well-being.

Its main innovations are:

  • Movement-Debt Index (MDI): A transparent score that combines static time, pressure concentration, verified movement breaks, and exercise adherence.
  • Gravity-aware recommendations: The system adapts guidance for microgravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, and Earth gravity.
  • Optional smart seat: The chair adds value without making the entire system dependent on specialized hardware.
  • Offline-first design: The dashboard and core functions work without cloud connectivity or continuous Earth communication.
  • Privacy-preserving architecture: No camera, no microphone, and no automatic cloud transmission of raw personal data.
  • Radiation-aware fail-safe design: The system separates low-cost sensing from trusted decision-making and degrades safely if electronics fail.
  • Interactive body map: Helps users understand which body region may be associated with a logged indicator or discomfort pattern.

Factors considered

The team considered several important factors:

  • Astronaut autonomy: Crew members need tools that work during communication delays and do not depend on Earth support.
  • Privacy: Health data must remain private, with local processing and explicit user control over data export.
  • Usability: Alerts must be helpful rather than disruptive; haptic feedback and simple visuals reduce interruption.
  • Safety: The system must never interfere with emergency movement, restraint systems, or medical care.
  • Power efficiency: The ESP32 uses duty-cycled sensing and low-power modes to extend battery life.
  • Radiation resilience: The design accounts for cumulative radiation effects, single-event faults, and potential latch-up conditions.
  • Scalability: The platform can begin with crew-entered data and later add more sensors as validation and mission requirements evolve.
  • Regulatory boundaries: PosturePilot supports wellness, self-assessment, and routine adherence; it does not make diagnostic or treatment claims.
